\section[el novio]{el novio — the boyfriend; the groom}

\label{lesson:ES-C547-novio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the grandson, then the Spanish for the nappy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el novio}
\textbf{el novio} — \textquotedblleft{}the boyfriend; the groom\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Su novio es de Bogotá.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Her boyfriend is from Bogotá.}
\end{quote}

On the wedding day \emph{el novio} is the groom, and \emph{los novios} are the couple.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{novio} is inherited from spoken Latin \emph{*novius} 'newly married' (EtymDB), built on \emph{novus} 'new'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el novio}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el novio}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el novio}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the grandson, then the Spanish for the nappy, then say \emph{el novio} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el novio mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The boyfriend; the groom\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la novia]{la novia — the girlfriend; the bride}

\label{lesson:ES-C547-novia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the nappy, then the Spanish for the boyfriend.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la novia}
\textbf{la novia} — \textquotedblleft{}the girlfriend; the bride\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La novia llevaba un vestido azul.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The bride wore a blue dress.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{novia} is the feminine of \emph{novio}, inherited from spoken Latin \emph{*novius}, \emph{*novia} 'newly married', built on \emph{novus} 'new' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[comprometerse]{comprometerse — to get engaged; to commit oneself}

\label{lesson:ES-C547-comprometerse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the boyfriend, then the Spanish for the girlfriend.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: comprometerse}
\textbf{comprometerse} — \textquotedblleft{}to get engaged; to commit oneself\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Se comprometieron en Navidad.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{They got engaged at Christmas.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Comprometerse a} + infinitive is to promise to: \emph{Me comprometo a ayudar.}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{comprometerse} comes from Latin \emph{comprōmittere} 'to promise each other' (Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{com-} and \emph{prōmittere} 'to promise', from \emph{mittere} 'to send'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[el compromiso]{el compromiso — the engagement; the commitment}

\label{lesson:ES-C547-compromiso}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the girlfriend, then the Spanish for to get engaged.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el compromiso}
\textbf{el compromiso} — \textquotedblleft{}the engagement; the commitment\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Anunciaron su compromiso en la cena.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{They announced their engagement at dinner.}
\end{quote}

A false friend: compromise is \emph{el acuerdo} or \emph{la concesión}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{compromiso} comes from Latin \emph{comprōmissum} 'a mutual promise' (EtymDB), built on \emph{prōmittere} 'to promise', from \emph{mittere} 'to send'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[el anillo]{el anillo — the ring}

\label{lesson:ES-C547-anillo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to get engaged, then the Spanish for the engagement.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el anillo}
\textbf{el anillo} — \textquotedblleft{}the ring\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Le regaló un anillo de oro.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He gave her a gold ring.}
\end{quote}

\emph{El anillo de compromiso} — the engagement ring.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{anillo} is inherited from Latin \emph{ānellus} 'a little ring' (EtymDB), a small form of \emph{ānulus} 'ring'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
